Volume 11 · Chapter 01

Financial intermediation and bank economics

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v06, v07, v09, v10

By the endExplain the economic functions and fragilities of financial intermediaries.

Volume 11 · Chapter 1

Financial intermediation and bank economics

A lender can select a profitable set of borrowers and still fail to make a payment tomorrow. A deposit contract can improve households’ consumption insurance and still invite a run. To explain these outcomes, follow four different objects: information, incentives, balance-sheet claims and cash available at a particular date. This chapter develops small models in which each object can be checked.

Capability. Explain screening and monitoring with explicit decisions and costs; reconcile loan and deposit creation; separate interest income, profit, capital and settlement cash; and prove both a useful liquidity allocation and a run equilibrium under stated withdrawal rights. All numerical cases are original synthetic teaching cases, not observations about a real institution.

Prerequisites. Use conditional probability and expected utility from Volume 3; incentives and best replies from Volume 5; the monetary balance sheets of Volume 6, Chapter 6; the double entry and cash-flow distinctions of Volume 7, Chapter 1 and Chapter 2; and the distinction between physical probabilities and market state prices in Volume 9, Chapter 5. The dated funding discipline of Volume 10, Chapter 6 continues to apply. No stochastic calculus or unproved banking-equilibrium theorem is required here.

1. The services and the claims

A financial intermediary stands between claim holders and the users of funds. It can investigate applicants, enforce a contract after funding, collect payments, diversify exposures, provide payment services, and issue claims whose timing differs from that of its assets. These functions can coexist, but one does not prove the others valuable. A passive fund that passes asset values through to its investors has different redemption promises from a bank offering deposits payable at par on demand.

Screening uses information before a lending decision to distinguish prospective risks. Monitoring observes or constrains conduct after the loan is made. Hidden borrower characteristics and hidden borrower actions are therefore different problems. A perfectly accurate report about yesterday’s conduct is not automatically an enforceable remedy for tomorrow’s diversion. An intermediary also needs incentives to perform the monitoring it promises.

A deposit is the bank’s liability to its customer. Reserves in our ledger are the bank’s settlement asset; customers cannot spend them directly. A loan is the bank’s claim on a borrower. Book equity is recorded assets minus recorded liabilities. It is a residual claim and an accounting loss buffer, not a separate cash account. The value obtainable by selling assets, the value of promised future payments, and the cash actually deployable before a deadline can all differ from book amounts.

Maturity transformation finances assets that deliver later with claims that can demand payment earlier. Its economic attraction requires explanation: why do customers value the early-payment right, and what makes the asset hard to turn into cash? Its fragility requires a second explanation: who can withdraw, in what order, at what price, and using which assets? A balance-sheet total alone answers neither question.

2. Screening as a decision about conditional cash receipts

Consider dates 0 and 1. A risk-neutral lender can advance principal L and receive F upon project success or recovery H upon failure, with 0≤H<F. Funds have a zero safe opportunity rate in this example. The lender may refuse the loan, earning zero. There are no other loan costs or portfolio constraints. If the physical success probability conditional on available information is p, expected loan surplus is

g(p)=pF+(1−p)H−L=H+(F−H)p−L.
Fund when g(p)>0, equivalently p>(L−H)/(F−H).

At equality the lender is indifferent; our lab resolves the tie by refusing. A threshold below zero makes every nonnegative p weakly acceptable, while a threshold above one makes every p unacceptable. These are decision calculations under specified risk neutrality and funding costs, not arbitrage prices. A risk-averse, capital-constrained lender or a nonzero funding rate would need a different objective or hurdle. These probabilities are physical beliefs; they are not the Q probabilities of derivative replication.

Worked example 1: a useful test that does not remove default risk

An applicant needs L=100; F=120 and H=20. Quality is good with prior probability 3/5 and bad with probability 2/5. Success probabilities are 19/20 and 9/20 respectively. A test passes 4/5 of good applicants and 1/5 of bad applicants. Conditional on quality, the test outcome supplies no further information about project success. Testing costs 3 at date 0 for every applicant tested, including those subsequently refused. Borrowers cannot manipulate the test.

Without a test, success probability is (3/5)(19/20)+(2/5)(9/20)=3/4. Expected receipt is 20+100(3/4)=95. The loan loses 5 in expectation; refusing earns zero. Funding requires p>4/5.

The joint masses of good-pass and bad-pass are 12/25 and 2/25. A pass therefore occurs with probability 14/25 and has good-quality posterior (12/25)/(14/25)=6/7. Its success probability is (6/7)(19/20)+(1/7)(9/20)=123/140. Expected receipt is 755/7≈107.857143 and surplus per funded pass is 55/7. A fail occurs with probability 11/25 and has good posterior 3/11, success probability 129/220, receipt 865/11≈78.636364 and surplus −235/11. Lend only after a pass.

Expected surplus per tested applicant = (14/25)(55/7)−3 = 22/5−3 = 7/5 = 1.4.

The relevant cost denominator is all tested applicants. Charging the test only to approved loans would understate cost. If one allocates total test cost across approved loans for reporting, it is 3/(14/25)=75/14 per funded loan; subtracting it from 55/7 leaves 5/2 per funded loan, which gives 1.4 when multiplied by 14/25. The success probability of approved loans remains below one. A profitable selection policy does not promise that any particular approved loan repays.

Value-of-information proof. Let a finite signal s have probability ms, with conditional expected loan surplus gs. Ignore zero-probability signals. By total expectation the no-signal surplus of lending is g=Σmsgs. The best no-test value is max(g,0); the best gross value with the signal is V=Σmsmax(gs,0). Since max(gs,0)≥gs and ≥0, V≥g and V≥0, hence V≥max(g,0). Free information cannot lower this decision maker’s value because it can be ignored. A test costing k is preferred exactly when V−max(g,0)>k. In this case the maximum worthwhile cost is 22/5=4.4, with indifference at that cost.

The proof requires the same projects and feasible decisions before and after receiving information. It does not cover a test that changes borrower behavior, a test whose errors depend on later actions, or an undisclosed obligation to lend after testing. It is a private decision value, not a social-welfare theorem: borrower benefits, external costs and the origin of screening costs would also matter. In practice, estimation error, changed applicants and strategic manipulation require evidence beyond a confusion matrix fitted on previously approved loans.

3. Monitoring, free riding and the monitor’s own incentives

Pooling claims can avoid duplicated investigation, but that observation is incomplete without specifying how an investigator changes outcomes and who pays. Diamond’s delegated-monitoring exposition analyzes monitoring costs together with the cost of inducing an intermediary to perform its task. The following finite example isolates those two costs. It does not import the paper’s optimal-debt or diversification results.

Worked example 2: enforcement that changes an action

A project costs 100 now and produces 140 on success or zero on failure at date 1. Debt promises 120 in success; limited liability makes both lender and borrower receive zero from the project in failure. The risk-neutral borrower chooses a prudent action with success probability .9 or diversion with success probability .6 and a private benefit worth 8 utility units. The private benefit is not cash available to creditors. The borrower keeps 20 in success. Its prudent expected payoff is .9(20)=18; diversion gives .6(20)+8=20. It diverts.

A verifiable enforcement action costs 5 and removes the private diversion benefit before the choice is made. The low-success action then gives .6(20)=12, below 18, so prudence is strictly preferred. This is a contractual intervention with the specified power; merely purchasing an adverse report would not produce the same result. Expected debt receipts rise from .6(120)=72 to .9(120)=108, a gain of 36.

Suppose 12 equal direct claimants already hold the loan. Any one can purchase the same nonexclusive enforcement; one intervention benefits all claimants and duplicates add nothing. When all others abstain, the payer gains only 36/12=3 from its claim and pays 5. Abstaining is strictly better. If someone else already enforces, an additional intervention has zero benefit and positive cost. Thus no enforcement is a Nash equilibrium of this post-funding monitoring game. It is not an equilibrium claim that rational lenders originally finance a loan whose anticipated receipts are only 72 for an outlay of 100.

Now a pooled vehicle can commit to the intervention. It raises 100 for the project, 5 for enforcement and 1 for an observable completion check with payment conditional on completion. Its initial funding need is 106, and expected receipt is 108; its surplus is 2 at the zero opportunity rate. The commitment and completion-check technology are assumptions, not free consequences of calling the vehicle a bank. Without them, a paid monitor could shirk. All 12 claimants separately buying enforcement would cost 60 and yield 108−100−60=−52; their unmonitored loan would yield 72−100=−28. Refusing finance remains worth zero.

The exact thresholds. With N equal claimants, no enforcement is a best reply to none by others when 36/N≤5; for integer N the inequality holds from N=8 onward. A pooled vehicle with delegation cost d has surplus 108−100−5−d=3−d, so it is financeable on these terms for d≤3, with zero surplus at equality. The cost advantage of avoiding N−1 duplicate interventions is a different comparison; a vehicle can be cheaper than duplication and still have negative total surplus. Borrower prudence without enforcement requires 18≥12+b, or private benefit b≤6. At b=6 our stated tie convention selects prudence; there is then no improvement in repayment from enforcement.

The calculations reveal what evidence would be needed: action-dependent repayment, enforceability, who captures the gain, cost, and the credibility of the delegated task. They do not show that every financial intermediary exists for this reason, that a larger pool eliminates correlated losses, or that a monitored loan is safe. The later credit-analysis chapter develops repayment sources and covenant responses; this example supplies the incentive logic those procedures need.

4. A loan creates a deposit; a payment creates a funding question

Use a simple book-value identity A=R+L=D+E: assets consist of settlement reserves R and loans L; funding consists of deposits D and equity E. There are no allowances, securities, taxes, other liabilities or valuation changes in the opening ledger. Each bank’s initial accounts balance. A loan credited to its borrower’s account increases L and D by the same amount, leaving R and E unchanged. This is the accounting mechanism described in the Bank of England’s 2014 money-creation article; the historical source is not being used to assert current universal reserve rules or central-bank lending terms.

Worked example 3: creation, settlement, income and a missed deadline

Amounts are currency units. A begins with reserves 24, loans 126, deposits 132 and equity 18. B begins with reserves 16, loans 64, deposits 72 and equity 8. A grants a new loan of 36 by crediting its borrower’s A deposit. The borrower then pays 24 to a seller whose account is at B. Settlement is immediate and final: A sends 24 reserves to B, removes 24 from its borrower’s deposit, and B credits the seller’s deposit by 24.

Two-bank ledger before any subsequent income
Event / bankReservesLoansAssetsDepositsEquity
Initial A2412615013218
Initial B166480728
A after origination2416218616818
A after external settlement016216214418
B after external settlement4064104968
A+B after external settlement4022626624026

Consolidated deposits rose from 204 to 240 on origination; the later payment merely relocated them. Consolidated reserves stayed 40 throughout. Loan creation neither used up 36 previously collected deposits nor manufactured new settlement reserves. A can create its deposit liability but cannot settle an arbitrary outward payment using that liability alone. The within-system conservation statement assumes precisely these two banks and this payment; currency withdrawals, central-bank operations and transactions beyond this boundary would add entries.

The immediate cutoff. Just after the 24 settlement, before any later receipts, an additional depositor requests an external payment of 5. A has zero available reserves and no borrowing, asset-sale or other cash facility in this probe. The request exceeds available cash by 5 even though book equity is 18. The probe is a failed request, not a transaction secretly posted as negative reserves. This timing is essential: later receipts cannot retrospectively meet this deadline.

Now consider a separate continuation without that additional withdrawal. Over the following one-year income period A receives external loan interest of 10 and fees of 2, then pays interest of 1.5 and operating cash costs of 3.5 externally, in that order. Principal repayments, deposit principal movements and dividends are zero. Income and expenses are recognized when these specified cash flows occur. Finally, a confirmed loan loss of 5 is recorded directly, with no prior allowance covering it. Loans and equity fall by 5; current cash does not. This simplified direct-loss treatment is not a statement about a particular accounting standard.

Net interest income = 10−1.5 = 8.5.
Profit = 10+2−1.5−3.5−5 = 2.
Closing reserves = 0+10+2−1.5−3.5 = 7.
Closing loans = 162−5 = 157; closing equity = 18+2 = 20.
Closing assets 164 = deposits 144 + equity 20.

A’s final reserves of 7 could meet a new request for 5 at that later date. They do not erase the earlier gap. This continuation is a ledger for A with outside cash counterparties; we are not pretending that B’s earlier entries remain the complete system after those additional external transactions. With an existing sufficient loan-loss allowance, a charge-off against that allowance would not record the same loss in income again; Chapter 2 develops that distinction.

Profit rates need denominators and periods. For this specified one-year continuation, define each average balance as the arithmetic mean of its opening and closing book values, not a claim about actual daily averages. Average earning loans are (162+157)/2=159.5; average total assets are (162+164)/2=163; average equity is (18+20)/2=19. Then

Net interest margin (NIM) = 8.5/159.5 = 17/319 ≈ 5.3292%;
return on assets (ROA) = 2/163 ≈ 1.2270%;
return on equity (ROE) = 2/19 ≈ 10.5263%.

These are annual case ratios, not regulatory measures. Gross loan yield is 10/159.5, whereas the deposit funding rate is 1.5/144. Their difference is not NIM, because the two component rates use different bases. Positive NIM does not cover credit losses, operating expenses or taxes automatically. Leverage can raise ROE on a profitable asset book while increasing the impact of losses on equity. If average equity is zero or negative, this lab returns no ROE; a mechanically calculated ratio would obscure the capital problem.

Capital and cash can move together or separately. At the immediate cutoff, an externally settled equity subscription of 5 adds 5 reserves and 5 equity. External borrowing of 5 adds 5 reserves and a new debt liability, leaving equity unchanged. Either supplies the missing cash if completed before the deadline and contractually available. Converting 5 of an existing A deposit into equity reduces D by 5 and raises E by 5 but creates no reserves. A direct uncovered loan loss reduces equity without a current cash outflow. These entries explain why neither “capital is cash” nor “capital has nothing to do with funding” is satisfactory: the transaction and date determine the connection.

5. Liquidity insurance under a stated withdrawal contract

We now isolate timing risk from credit loss. This is a separate three-date mutual institution, not A or B from the preceding ledger. Diamond and Dybvig’s original model motivates the combination of private consumption needs, sequential deposit service and illiquid investment. We specify our own utility, parameters and proofs; no optimal-contract or deposit-insurance theorem is assumed.

At date 0 a nonatomic population of total mass 100 deposits one consumption unit per member. “Mass 100” is a continuum of arbitrarily small claimants, not exactly 100 indivisible accounts: one person’s deviation does not change aggregate withdrawals. The mutual invests all 100 in a long asset. Each unit liquidated at date 1 yields ℓ=1 then and nothing later; each unit retained yields R=1.5 at date 2. Partial liquidation is allowed. There is no credit uncertainty, secondary market, outside borrowing, deposit insurance or suspension of withdrawals. Private storage carries one unit from date 1 to date 2 at gross return one.

At date 1 each depositor privately learns whether it is early or late. The known aggregate early fraction is λ=1/4; ex ante each person has that probability of being early. Early types value only date-1 consumption; late types value only date-2 consumption and can store an early withdrawal. Both use u(c)=−1/(c+.1), c≥0. It is increasing and strictly concave since u′(c)=1/(c+.1)²>0 and u″(c)=−2/(c+.1)³<0, and u(0)=−10 is finite. No assumption about independent finite-sample counts is needed: the aggregate mass is specified exactly.

The mutual promises c1=1.1 per unit deposit requested at date 1, subject to assets being available. Each depositor must choose either full withdrawal or waiting. A type-blind random queue is formed after withdrawal decisions; a requester’s rank is uniform within the mass of requests. The mutual liquidates only as needed and serves claims sequentially until assets are exhausted; unserved requesters receive zero and have no residual asset to claim when exhaustion occurs. Those who wait divide all remaining date-2 proceeds equally per initial deposit. Thus 1.1 is the early claim, while the late payment is residual, not an independently guaranteed promise.

Worked example 4: better insurance and a second equilibrium

First suppose only the 25 early types withdraw. Paying them 25(1.1)=27.5 uses 27.5 long-asset units. The remaining 72.5 yield 108.75 at date 2, or 108.75/75=1.45 per waiting late type. A late person could instead withdraw and store 1.1, but prefers 1.45. An early person gets nothing useful by waiting, so prefers withdrawal. These are best replies to the specified aggregate behavior; this is a no-run equilibrium after deposits have been made.

For comparison, without the mutual an individual can hold the long asset directly: early consumption is 1, late consumption 1.5. At ℓ=1, storing at date 0 cannot improve either outcome, so all-long direct holding is a best feasible autarky plan in this model without trade or private insurance. The no-run contract transfers some late consumption to early consumption. Compute expected utility before types are known:

EUdirect=−(1/4)/(1+.1)−(3/4)/(1.5+.1)=−245/352≈−.696023;
EUno-run=−(1/4)/(1.1+.1)−(3/4)/(1.45+.1)=−515/744≈−.692204.
EUno-run−EUdirect=125/32736>0.

The feasible contract improves ex ante utility under the no-run behavior. It has not been proved optimal. Its aggregate date-2 production is lower because it supplies more early consumption; that resource cost is included in the utility comparison.

Now suppose all other depositors withdraw. Liquidation supplies only 100 at date 1, while claims total 110. The queue serves mass 100/1.1=1000/11; a requester receives 1.1 with probability 10/11 and zero otherwise. A single late person who waits cannot prevent exhaustion and receives zero. Joining the queue gives

EUjoin=(10/11)u(1.1)+(1/11)u(0)=−5/3 > −10=u(0)=EUwait.

The late person therefore strictly prefers to join; an early person also prefers this positive chance of early consumption to none. All-withdraw is another post-deposit equilibrium under these rights. Expected consumption of a requester is one, but expected utility is −5/3, not u(1)=−10/11. Averaging the cash before applying a concave utility function would erase the queue risk.

Deriving the withdrawal threshold. For a general withdrawal fraction w∈[λ,1), the mutual needs 100wc1 early cash. When wc1≤ℓ it liquidates fraction wc1/ℓ of its initial assets. Waiting consumption is therefore

c2(w)=R·max(1−wc1/ℓ,0)/(1−w).
Full early service is possible up to wcapacity=ℓ/c1.
For ℓ<c1<R, c2(w)=c1 at w*= (R−c1)/[c1(R/ℓ−1)].

Before capacity is exhausted, differentiation gives c′2(w)=R(1−c1/ℓ)/(1−w)²<0. Also 0<w*<ℓ/c1, because c1>ℓ. Hence late types prefer waiting below w*, are indifferent at w*, and prefer withdrawing above w* while service remains certain. Once w exceeds capacity, waiting pays zero but joining still gives a positive service probability. In the example, w*=8/11 and capacity=10/11. Waiting consumption is 1.45 at w=.25, 1.35 at .5, and .9 at .8. A profitable long asset does not keep early withdrawal incentives stable as other claimants run.

At w=1 there are no actual waiters, so the formula’s denominator is zero. Do not report a fictitious average payment to them. The lab returns null for that average and separately reports zero consumption for a hypothetical atomless late deviation, justified by exhaustion when the other claimants run. A finite bank with large depositors, a known priority position, early withdrawal fees, partial withdrawals or new asset-sale rights would require a different game.

The equilibrium statements are conditional on deposits already being in place. A person certain at date 0 of a later run need not choose to deposit. We have not supplied an equilibrium-selection theory, an estimated run probability, or proof that this mutual is the globally best financial arrangement. Deposit insurance, suspension and emergency lending change rights, incentives and resource support; their effects must be derived under their own assumptions. Detailed liquidity ladders and systemic feedback are reserved for Chapters 5 and 11. No contemporary legal guarantee is implied by this uninsured toy model.

6. Reproduce the mechanisms and interrogate the assumptions

Download the synthetic inputs, Python model, exact output, SHA256 manifest and instructions and domain. Keeping those five files together, run python3 v11-c01-analysis.py --input v11-c01-inputs.json --output result.json. Paths can be absolute; no network or packages are needed. Importing the module or calling run(data) produces no console output and does not modify the input. Output rationals are strings, preserving exact arithmetic.

The four cases are separate economic mechanisms within one bounded lab, not one invented bank with incompatible contracts. The model checks both screening branches, borrower and claimant incentives, every two-bank entry and subsequent A cash entry, and the claimant mass, liquidation and queue utility at each requested withdrawal fraction. The README specifies bounded rational strings, a maximum of 16 withdrawal scenarios and the economic inequalities for the supported run contract. A zero-probability test branch has null conditional statistics. Undefined ratios and the absent full-run waiter average are also null.

Financially adverse results are not automatically malformed inputs. A costly test can be rejected, delegated monitoring can lose money, a valid bank loss can make book equity negative, and an early-type fraction can make the proposed no-run allocation incentive-incompatible. The model reports those results. It rejects a claimed executed bank payment requiring an unspecified funding facility, while the separate immediate-withdrawal probe is expressly allowed to fail. Reducing ℓ below one makes direct all-long investment merely a comparison plan; it need not remain optimal relative to private storage. Exact arithmetic validates the specified calculation, not these assumptions.

Try three interventions before reading the solutions: raise the test cost above 4.4; reduce the monitoring game to six claimants; and raise requested withdrawals to .8. Then move the immediate payment deadline to the end of the income period on paper. The causal lesson is different in each case: information cost, the share of an enforcement benefit, strategic withdrawal incentives, and cash timing. A general statement that “risk increased” would lose the mechanism needed for a decision.

7. Exercises

  1. Transfer: a changed applicant pool. In Worked example 1 change only the good-type prior to 1/2. Derive pass and fail masses, both quality posteriors, both success probabilities and the optimal conditional lending decisions. Compare the test policy at cost 3 with the best no-test decision, and find the maximum worthwhile test cost. Explain why reusing the old 6/7 posterior would be a substantive mistake.
  2. Proof and cost accounting. Prove the finite-signal gross value-of-information inequality for the lend/refuse choice, including zero-probability branches. For the original example, show why 3 per tested applicant and 75/14 per funded loan represent the same total cost. If the test cost is exactly 4.4, which policies maximize value? Does a screening gain prove a social-welfare improvement?
  3. Monitoring incentives and delegation. Use Worked example 2. With six equal claimants, is no enforcement a Nash equilibrium after funding? Show whether a profile with exactly one enforcing claimant is an equilibrium. Find the largest delegation cost that permits nonnegative pooled surplus. Finally set the private benefit to 6, taking prudence at a tie: compare unmonitored lending with the original pooled arrangement. Explain why a report that merely reveals diversion cannot be substituted for the assumed enforcement.
  4. Two-bank transfer. Return to the initial A and B balance sheets, but let A originate 18 and its borrower immediately pay all 18 to a B depositor. Reconcile both banks, system deposits and reserves, and A’s equity/assets ratio. Can the immediate 5 withdrawal now be met? Do not post that probe in the main ledger. Repeat A’s balance-sheet totals if the borrower instead pays a seller who already banks at A, and explain the settlement difference.
  5. Income, losses and a cash capital raise. Return to the original 36 loan and 24 external payment. Recompute all three annual ratios stated in Section 4. Replace the final direct loss of 5 first by 22 and then by 26: calculate closing cash, loans, equity and profit, and the loss that leaves zero equity. Separately, at the immediate cutoff before income, compare (a) a 5 external equity subscription, (b) 5 external borrowing due later and (c) conversion of 5 existing deposits into equity. Which changes equity, which supplies the missing 5 cash, and what happens after executing the withdrawal in (a) and (b)?
  6. Proof: the fragile withdrawal threshold. For 0<ℓ<c1<R and a nonatomic population, derive c2(w), the capacity fraction and w*. Prove w* lies below capacity and that waiting consumption decreases before exhaustion. Calculate the three quantities for ℓ=1, R=3/2, c1=11/10. At an early fraction λ=4/5, can “only early types withdraw” be a no-run equilibrium even though all their early claims can be paid?
  7. Queue risk and what has been proved. Reproduce both ex ante utility values and their difference in Worked example 4. Reproduce the full-run join-versus-wait utility comparison. Explain why u(expected cash) is the wrong criterion here, why a single late deviation leaves exhaustion unchanged, and why these calculations do not prove that households voluntarily deposit when certain of a run. What additional optimization issue appears if ℓ falls below one?
  8. Decision memo and evidence critique. A manager writes: “The tested loans are safe because expected receipts exceed principal. Monitoring reports ensure good conduct. Positive NIM and equity guarantee tomorrow’s withdrawals. A loan consumes pre-existing customer deposits. Our no-run utility gain proves the deposit contract optimal and deposit insurance always costless.” Replace all six assertions with conditional, testable statements. Propose one validation action for screening, one for monitoring and one for dated funding, naming a limitation of each. Give a defensible response to the immediate 5 payment request without assuming an uncommitted facility exists.
Complete solutions and assessment criteria

  1. Pass mass is (.5)(.8)+(.5)(.2)=.5, with good posterior .4/.5=.8. Success probability is (.8)(.95)+(.2)(.45)=.85; receipt is 105 and loan surplus 5, so lend. Fail mass is .5, good posterior .1/.5=.2, success probability (.2)(.95)+(.8)(.45)=.55; receipt is 75 and surplus −25, so refuse. The pooled success probability is .7, receipt 90 and loan surplus −10; the best no-test value is zero. Testing gives .5(5)−3=−.5 per applicant, so choose no test and no lending. Maximum worthwhile test cost is 2.5, with a tie at equality. A posterior combines a likelihood with the prior: the same test properties do not preserve 6/7 when applicant composition changes. The conditional independence of test and success given type is still required.

  2. For every positive-mass signal define gs=E[repayment−L|s]. Total expectation gives g=Σmsgs. Each positive part is at least the original number and at least zero; summing gives V=Σmsmax(gs,0)≥max(g,0). A zero-mass branch contributes zero and needs no conditional probability; assigning an invented posterior is unnecessary. Net information value is V−max(g,0)−k, so gross nonnegativity does not guarantee value after costs. In the original case the funded mass is 14/25 and (14/25)(75/14)=3, the cost paid across all applicants. Surplus per funded loan is 55/7−75/14=5/2; multiplying by 14/25 gives 7/5. At k=22/5 both refusal without a test and testing then lending only on passes yield zero; mixtures of those policies are also optimal. Lending to the untested pool or to failed applicants loses value. No social-welfare comparison follows without borrower utility, resource costs and external effects; transfers such as interest are not automatically social costs.

  3. With N=6 one claimant gains 36/6=6 by enforcing when nobody else does, and pays 5. Abstaining from enforcement is therefore not a best reply in the all-abstain profile. With exactly one enforcer, that claimant loses a net 1 if it quits; each other claimant would waste 5 by duplicating an intervention that adds no further repayment. Thus any profile with exactly one enforcer is a Nash equilibrium of the specified post-funding game. The pooled surplus with delegation cost d is 3−d, giving d≤3 for nonnegative surplus. With benefit b=6, prudent payoff 18 equals diversion payoff 12+6=18; the specified tie selects prudence. Unmonitored receipt is already 108 and surplus 8. The original pooled arrangement still costs 106 and yields surplus 2, so it is inferior by its unnecessary cost of 6. A report alone changes neither available action nor private benefit in this payoff table. One must establish an enforceable response before replacing the action payoffs.

  4. After origination A has R=24,L=144,D=150,E=18. Paying 18 externally gives A=(R,L,D,E)=(6,144,132,18), assets 150; B=(34,64,90,8), assets 98. System reserves remain 40, loans rise from 190 to 208, deposits from 204 to 222, and equity stays 26. A’s ratio is 18/150=.12. The probe for 5 is executable from 6, leaving 1 if actually made; the requested ledger does not include it. If the seller banks at A, the payment reallocates 18 between A customer accounts: A remains R=24,L=144,D=150,E=18, assets 168 and equity/assets=3/28≈10.7143%. B is unchanged. No interbank reserve transfer is required for that internal payment. Neither case removes the deposit newly created by origination from the system.

  5. Original NIM=(10−1.5)/[(162+157)/2]=17/319; ROA=2/[(162+164)/2]=2/163; ROE=2/[(18+20)/2]=2/19. These fractions become percentages by multiplying by 100 and apply to the specified one-year period and simple average balances. For any replacement direct loss x, cash is 7, loans 162−x, profit 7−x and equity 25−x. At x=22 these are 7,140,−15 and 3 respectively; at x=26 they are 7,136,−19 and −1. The zero-equity loss is 25. Cash sufficient for a later 5 payment can coexist with negative book equity, just as positive equity coexisted with the earlier cash gap.

    At the immediate cutoff the opening entries are R=0,L=162,D=144,E=18. External equity adds cash and equity: R=5,L=162,D=144,E=23. After paying the 5 withdrawal, R=0,L=162,D=139,E=23. External borrowing instead gives R=5,L=162,D=144,E=18 and new borrowing liability 5; after withdrawal R=0,D=139 with loans, equity and borrowing unchanged. It replaces some deposit funding by borrowed funding and creates a later repayment obligation. Conversion of existing deposits gives R=0,L=162,D=139,E=23: it raises equity but cannot settle the separate external request for 5. The first two answers assume financing is actually received before the deadline, with no omitted issuance cost; an intention to raise funds does not add cash.

  6. Per initial deposit the requested early cash is wc1. It requires wc1/ℓ asset units until that number reaches one. The remaining max(1−wc1/ℓ,0) units yield R times that amount, divided among mass 1−w; this gives c2(w). Capacity is ℓ/c1. Before capacity, set R(1−wc1/ℓ)=c1(1−w) and solve for w*=(R−c1)/[c1(R/ℓ−1)]. All factors in its numerator and denominator are positive. The inequality w*<ℓ/c1 is equivalent to R−c1<R−ℓ, which holds. Differentiating the quotient gives R(1−c1/ℓ)/(1−w)²<0. At the stated parameters capacity=10/11, w*=8/11 and c2(w)=(3/2)(1−11w/10)/(1−w) before exhaustion. With λ=.8, early cash .88 is feasible but waiting consumption is .9. A late person can get and store 1.1 by withdrawing, so the proposed no-run behavior is not an equilibrium. Feasibility alone does not establish incentives.

  7. Direct holding gives −(1/4)(10/11)−(3/4)(5/8)=−245/352. No-run consumption gives −(1/4)(5/6)−(3/4)(20/31)=−515/744; subtracting yields 125/32736>0. In a full run the service probability is 10/11, so expected utility is (10/11)(−5/6)+(1/11)(−10)=−5/3. Waiting gives −10. By contrast, expected cash is (10/11)(11/10)=1 and u(1)=−10/11, which exceeds actual lottery utility because u is strictly concave and the outcomes differ. The agent is atomless: removing its own request does not reduce the other requests below the exhaustion threshold 10/11. This proves its best reply after deposits are fixed. It does not solve the earlier participation decision; someone certain of the run compares −5/3 with the better direct-holding outcome and would prefer not to deposit. If ℓ<1, storage at date 0 can protect early consumption at a cost to late returns. All-long direct investment is no longer shown to be the optimal autarky portfolio, so its utility alone is not an adequate best-alternative benchmark.

  8. Illustrative response. Approved loans have positive expected margin under stated probabilities, costs and risk neutrality, but still default with positive probability. A monitoring report improves conduct only if detection is linked to a credible incentive or intervention. NIM excludes other costs, book equity is not deployable cash, and payments need a dated funding plan. Origination credits a deposit and records a loan; subsequent external settlement requires reserves or another available facility. The utility calculation establishes one feasible improvement under one no-run equilibrium, not contract optimality. Insurance changes incentives and resource obligations; neither its terms nor its costs have been modeled.

    For screening, audit outcome definitions and estimate performance on a separately observed applicant cohort, addressing rejected applicants whose repayment outcomes are missing; an approved-only backtest does not identify unconditional test value. For monitoring, verify completion and the legal and operational ability to prevent the modeled diversion, then compare behavior under a credible design; a completion stamp alone does not establish causal effectiveness. For funding, reconcile the time-stamped available-cash ledger to executable, unencumbered resources and test receipt delays; a single successful scenario does not cover future correlated withdrawals. At the immediate cutoff, record an unfilled 5 request and escalate the gap. A concrete remedy may be a verified external cash capital subscription, an available borrowing facility or a realizable asset sale received in time. Until one is actually available, none belongs in the executable cash balance.

    Rubric, 12 points: one for each of the six corrected statements; one each for three operational validation actions with their limitations; two for reconciling the zero-cash deadline and a conditional, executable funding remedy; one for separating model proof from empirical or legal evidence. An answer that retrospectively funds the immediate payment with later income, claims a guarantee of no default, or invents an already available facility requires correction regardless of its total score.

8. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back prompt. In three minutes, explain how a bank can create a deposit without creating equity or settlement reserves, and how useful intermediation can coexist with fragility. Include one screening calculation and one depositor best reply.

Model response. A new loan credits the borrower’s deposit and adds an equal loan asset. In our case 36 increases loans and deposits by 36 while equity stays 18 and reserves stay 24. Sending 24 to another bank then reduces A’s reserves to zero. The bank’s later profit cannot settle an earlier 5 deadline. Information can still be valuable: test-and-lend-on-pass yields (14/25)(55/7)−3=1.4 per applicant. Separately, the mutual provides 1.1 for early needs and 1.45 for late needs, improving ex ante utility. A late depositor waits when others do, but joins a full run because the queue offers a positive chance of payment whereas waiting after exhaustion pays zero. The benefit and fragility follow from specific cash and incentive assumptions, not contradictory descriptions of the same statistic.

Retention check, after one week without notes. (1) In the screening example, what is the maximum worthwhile test cost per applicant? (2) Does a borrower-deposit credit of 10 itself add 10 equity? (3) What does a confirmed uncovered loan loss of 4 do to cash and equity? (4) What withdrawal fraction exhausts the mutual’s assets? (5) Is a no-run allocation that pays early claims necessarily incentive-compatible? (6) Why can a deposit-to-equity conversion fail to cure an external payment gap?

Answers. (1) 4.4, with indifference there. (2) No: loans and deposits each rise 10. (3) It leaves current cash unchanged and reduces loans and equity by 4 in our no-prior-allowance treatment. (4) 10/11; every further request adds queue risk without new resources. (5) No: at w=.8 early claims are feasible but late waiting pays .9 instead of the obtainable 1.1. (6) It reclassifies a liability into equity without supplying settlement reserves. Revisit Section 2 for conditional probabilities, Section 3 for enforcement incentives, Section 4 for accounting and timing, and Section 5 for contractual best replies.

Source scope and next steps. The 1996 delegated-monitoring article, 2014 money-creation article and 1983 liquidity paper provide primary conceptual routes. The calculations, utility, cases and exercises here are original instructional constructions; the papers’ historical statistics, jurisdictional rules and broader optimality or policy results are not current claims of this chapter. Chapter 2 develops provisions, capital concepts and deployable liquidity; later chapters add borrower evidence, liquidity ladders, regulation and systemic interactions.

Sources and further study

  • Douglas W. Diamond — Financial Intermediation as Delegated Monitoring: A Simple Example, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Economic Quarterly 82(3), 51–66 (Summer 1996) — Primary conceptual route for avoiding duplicated monitoring and accounting for the cost of delegated incentives. The chapter proves its own finite enforcement/public-benefit game and financing comparison; it does not assume Diamond's optimal-debt or diversification results.
  • Douglas W. Diamond and Philip H. Dybvig — Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity, Journal of Political Economy 91(3), 401–419 (June 1983) — Primary source for private liquidity needs, sequential random service, mutual residual claims and post-deposit run best replies. Original utility, calibration and proof in the chapter establish only the stated feasible insurance comparison and two post-deposit equilibria; no optimal-insurance or policy theorem is imported.
  • Michael McLeay, Amar Radia and Ryland Thomas, Money creation in the modern economy, Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin 2014 Q1 — Official central-bank method explanation of loan-created deposits, reserve settlement, bank funding and risk constraints, loan repayment and bank/nonbank asset-purchase counterparts.
